implementation_notes: Rust's enum is the closed set: variants are declared together with their payload types, and match is exhaustiveness-checked by the compiler (E0004) unless the last arm is a wildcard, so the visitor and double-dispatch scaffolding never appears - operations are free functions or inherent methods that match on the value and usually take it by reference. #[non_exhaustive] is the deliberate escape hatch: outside the defining crate such an enum requires a catch-all arm, which is the honest way to publish an evolving set without pretending it is closed. Use the enum form whenever the set is closed and owned by the crate; when variants must come from other crates, keep a trait-object design instead, since match cannot be total over a trait.
pitfalls: A _ => arm anywhere recreates open behaviour and hides every variant added later, so wildcard arms over your own enums need a review rule or a lint that rejects them.
#[non_exhaustive] enums cannot be matched exhaustively outside their crate: the required wildcard arm turns coverage into a manual decision at every consumer.
E0004 is a hard error, so partial inspection has to use if let / let else or an explicit catch-all rather than an incomplete match.
